title: Will Educators Take YES! for an Answer?
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: This article addresses the major literacy communities -- Whole Language, Balanced Literacy, Structured Literacy, and Structured Word Inquiry -- with a 'YES...AND' framework, affirming the valid insights each camp holds while insisting each must also reckon with what it got wrong. Janetos argues that meaning matters (YES), but that reliable decoding is the prerequisite for meaning-making (AND); that balance is a real goal (YES), but that many 'balanced' classrooms over-relied on predictable text and memorization (AND); that phonics had been legitimately neglected (YES), but that structured literacy sometimes abandoned real reading and writing in connected text (AND). The essay critiques 'decoding denialism' -- the view that reading develops the same way as speaking -- and the alternative failure mode of drilling phonics while losing sight of comprehension and authentic reading contexts. A fourth section addresses Structured Word Inquiry, acknowledging its case for morphology while pushing back on the claim that morphological instruction can replace systematic phonics for beginning readers. The article models the kind of disciplined synthesis the literacy wars have resisted, framing the debate as a shared obligation to the full range of what literacy instruction requires.
points: The 'YES...AND' framework rejects the false choice between meaning and decoding: meaning is the goal of reading (YES), but reliable grapheme-phoneme decoding is the prerequisite (AND) -- it cannot be leapfrogged via context clues and pictures.

The Balanced Literacy critique: 'balance' became an excuse for imbalance -- word work was often serendipitous rather than sequenced, and guided reading with predictable text trained students to guess via sentence stems rather than actually decode.

The Structured Literacy critique: phonics instruction finally took its rightful place, but in many implementations application to real reading and writing in varied genres was abandoned in favor of phonics drills alone.

The Structured Word Inquiry section accepts the case for morphology instruction while pushing back on the claim that SWI's approach can serve as the primary route to word recognition for beginning readers.
The article's animating claim: 'reading does not develop the same way as speaking' -- rejecting Frank Smith's view -- so the decoding process must be explicitly taught and systematically sequenced.
quotes: We can't get to that meaning-making if we can't read the words: simple point but not a small matter. For many students, devaluing the decoding process can derail the whole enterprise. You were so right about the existence of graphophonic, syntactic, and semantic cues but so wrong about the order of operations.

If we leapfrog grapheme-phoneme connections to jump to meaning, we squander the opportunity to link phonology, orthography, and meaning in order to orthographically map the words we are decoding and make them available for future automatic word recognition.

Too often, classroom instruction was actually off-balance with books like predictable text because we prioritized the feat of getting through a book despite the self-defeating mechanism: memorization and guessing by completing sentence stems after looking at the pictures.
The science of reading had been sidelined, so we championed it and organized our reading instruction around the science, not the stories, behind how our brains learn to read.

Too often the application of foundational skills to real reading in a variety of text types and real writing in different genres was now left behind. Literacy components that were nice to know were treated as need to know.
Despite what Frank Smith said, reading does not develop the same way as speaking. We have to face this fact and reject decoding denialism.
